title: Leakage & Pacifiers
hook: The body does not betray secrets; it manages strain, and the hands that soothe a man point to the pressure without ever naming it.
why:
Most men learn about leakage from a television detective: the suspect touches his nose, the detective narrows his eyes, the case breaks. Real rooms are less obliging. Picture a quarterly review in which a project lead rubs the back of his neck every time the launch date comes up. His director, who has read a little about body language, decides the lead is hiding something and spends the meeting pressing him. The lead goes quieter, the director grows more certain, and the real problem, a dependency stuck in another team that the lead did not want to blame on a colleague, surfaces three weeks later as a missed launch.

What the director missed is that leakage is real but narrow. Under strain, the parts of the body we monitor least do show it, and self-soothing touches really do rise. What they tell you is where effort or discomfort has gathered, not what it is about, and certainly not whether someone is lying. Read well, a pacifier is a request for a gentler question. Read badly, it is a licence to interrogate, and interrogation produces exactly the signals that seem to confirm it.

teach.h: Leakage follows a gradient of control, not a map of secrets.
teach.p:
In 1969 Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen published a paper on what they called nonverbal leakage. Their argument was about sending capacity and feedback. The face can produce a huge range of fine distinctions, it is what other people watch most, and we get constant feedback about it, so it is the channel we manage best. The hands are watched less and the legs and feet hardly at all, so feeling that is being held back from the face is likelier to escape lower down. Ekman later argued that the face leaks too, in brief expressions, but the gradient itself remains a useful guide to where to look.

Notice what the gradient does and does not claim. It says unmanaged feeling is likelier to show in less-managed channels. It does not say that what shows was concealed, or guilty, or even emotional. A man smiling warmly while his foot taps under the table may be hiding impatience, or he may be someone whose foot always taps, or he may need the bathroom. Leakage is a property of channels, not a confession.

The most sobering numbers in this field come from Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo, who pooled more than two hundred studies of people judging truth from lies. Average accuracy was about 54 percent, a whisker above chance. DePaulo's own large review of behavioural cues to deception found most of them weakly related to lying, if at all. If leakage reliably revealed lies, those numbers would look very different.

So use the gradient as a viewing order, not a verdict. When you want to know how someone is actually doing, glance below the face, at the hands, shoulders, legs and feet. Then hold what you see as you would hold any other observation: against this person's baseline, in its timing, with an alternative explanation ready.
teach.disconfirm: If the lower channels of someone's body stay as calm as their face across the moments you care about, the gradient has nothing to show you, and you should stop looking for leakage that is not there. And if the change you see below the face also appears in moments of no consequence, it is part of their range.
teach.pullQuote: Leakage is a property of channels, not a confession.

teach.h: A pacifier is the body regulating itself, and it works.
teach.p:
Ekman and Friesen's 1969 catalogue of nonverbal behaviour named a class of movements they called adaptors: actions that once served the body's own needs, such as scratching, rubbing and holding, performed now in fragments. Self-adaptors, in which the hand touches the body, are what the former FBI agent Joe Navarro popularised as pacifying behaviours. The terms differ and the observation is the same. Under strain, people touch themselves more, and the touch does something.

There is reasonable evidence that it helps. Primatologists have long treated scratching and self-grooming as markers of anxiety in monkeys and apes, and the psychiatrist Alfonso Troisi reviewed this work and argued that the same displacement activities track stress in people. In 2013 Changiz Mohiyeddini and Stuart Semple put men through a standard laboratory stress test of public speaking and mental arithmetic and found that those who showed more displacement behaviour reported feeling less stressed. A group led by Martin Grunwald recorded brain activity while people held information in memory amid distracting noise, and found that spontaneous face touches were followed by changes they interpreted as regulation of attention and emotion.

The common forms are worth knowing so that you recognise them: a hand to the front of the neck, often over the hollow at the base of the throat; a palm rubbed across the back of the neck; fingers stroking the jaw, cheek or lips; palms pressed and slid down the thighs; one hand stroking the other forearm; a long exhale through puffed cheeks; fingers fiddling with a watch, ring, collar or cuff.

None of these is a symptom. Each is a small and effective act of self-care, and that framing matters for how you respond. When you see someone soothing themselves, you are watching them manage. You are not watching them crack.
teach.disconfirm: If self-touch in a particular person does not rise at moments you would expect to be hard for them, or rises just as much when they are relaxed and absorbed, it is not working as a pacifier in them. It is habit, grooming or simple comfort.
teach.pullQuote: You are watching them manage. You are not watching them crack.

teach.h: The base rate is high, so the rate is the signal.
teach.p:
Because self-touch is constant, a single instance tells you almost nothing. The medical students in Kwok's study touched their faces about 23 times an hour while doing nothing more stressful than attending a lecture. Jinni Harrigan, studying self-touching in the 1980s, found it bound up both with feeling and with the work of speaking and thinking: people touch themselves more when they are searching for words, not only when they are uneasy. A touch is as likely to mean *I am looking for the right phrase* as *I am uncomfortable*.

The informative quantity is the rate, measured against the person's own baseline. Suppose a man touches his face once or twice a minute through the easy part of a conversation. When a particular subject comes up he touches it seven times in the next minute, then gradually returns to his usual rate. That cluster, with its onset and its decay, is a pattern worth noticing. The touches themselves are unremarkable; the shape of the curve is what speaks.

This is also why the work cannot be done from a photograph. A still image of a hand at a throat is one frame from a rate you do not know. Newspapers love such frames, a politician caught mid-touch at the worst possible moment, and they mean almost nothing. The same politician may have touched his throat forty times that afternoon.

In practice, keep a rough count. You will not tally every touch in a live conversation, and you should not try; your attention belongs to the person. But you can notice, roughly, when someone moves from their ordinary rate to a great deal more, and when they come back down. The return matters too. A spike that settles suggests something registered and was absorbed. A rate that stays high suggests the pressure has stayed.
teach.disconfirm: If you cannot say what this person's ordinary rate of self-touch is, you cannot call any rate high. And if the cluster you noticed coincides with the person speaking at length or hunting for words, the effort of speech is a strong rival explanation.

teach.h: Timing turns a pacifier into a pointer.
teach.p:
A pacifier that arrives a second or two after a specific question, word or name is far more useful than one that drifts in over a minute. Timing turns a general sign of strain into a pointer: something about that moment cost this person effort.

The pointer is real but blunt. Suppose you ask a friend at dinner whether his father is out of hospital and whether he is still making the trip next month. His hand goes to the back of his neck before you finish. Which part landed? The father, the hospital, the trip, the cost of the trip, or your asking in front of other people? The body has told you where to look in time, not what you will find there.

You can sharpen a pointer without pressing on it. The method is gentle replication. Let the conversation move on and return to one element later, alone and in a different form: *how is your dad doing?* If the touch comes back with the father and not with the trip, you have learned something. If it comes back with neither, the first time may have been coincidence, or the moment may have passed. If it comes back whenever anything personal is raised, the issue may be talking about himself at all.

What you must not do is replicate by pressure: repeat the question harder, hold eye contact, wait in silence for the touch. That is an interrogation technique, and it fails on its own terms, because pressure produces pacifiers in honest, anxious people as reliably as in anyone. You will have manufactured the signal you were trying to read.

The aim of sharpening a pointer is never to catch someone. It is to know which question to ask kindly, or which subject to leave alone.
teach.disconfirm: If the touch does not recur when the same element returns in a calmer form, or recurs just as often with unrelated topics, the timing was coincidence or the pressure was general. One onset is an observation; a pattern needs at least two.
teach.pullQuote: The body has told you where to look in time, not what you will find there.

teach.h: Effort leaks too, and it looks like distress.
teach.p:
A great deal of what looks like emotional leakage is something else: effort. Thinking hard changes the body. People working to remember, calculate or find words often look away, slow down, pause, stop gesturing or touch their faces more. Arthur Glenberg and his colleagues found that averting the gaze helps people answer difficult questions, because faces and busy surroundings compete for the same attention. Susan Goldin-Meadow's research shows that gestures actively support thinking, so when speech gets hard some people gesture more while others go still.

Aldert Vrij built an approach to interviewing on this, arguing that lying is often harder work than telling the truth, so increasing the load on everyone, for instance by asking for an account in reverse order, makes a liar's extra effort easier to see. Whatever its merits in a police interview, the lesson for ordinary life runs the other way: honest people under load look a great deal like people under strain.

So when someone's hands stop and their eyes drop to the floor after your question, ask first whether the question was simply hard. Did you ask for a date, a number, a sequence, a judgment about something complicated? Did you ask in their second language, in a noisy room, at the end of a long day? Effort is the likeliest explanation for many of the changes this chapter teaches you to notice, and it is morally neutral.

Often the difference between effort and distress cannot be seen at all. Sometimes it shows in the recovery. Effort tends to resolve once the answer is found, often with a small release: a nod, a breath, the hands returning to their usual motion. Distress tends to linger past the answer. Even that is a tendency, not a rule.
teach.disconfirm: If the change persists after the person has found and given their answer, or appears with questions that need no thought at all, effort becomes a weaker explanation. If it resolves the moment they have their answer, assume effort first.

teach.h: Stillness can leak more than movement.
teach.p:
Popular body-language writing is obsessed with movement: the scratch, the touch, the shift. Experienced observers learn to watch for its absence. When someone who usually gestures goes still, when breathing seems to pause, when a bouncing foot suddenly stops, the body has done something as informative as any touch.

Stillness has several sources. Heavy thinking can freeze the hands, as the previous section showed. Alarm can too: many animals, people included, respond to a sudden threat by stopping, a response usually called freezing, which lets attention lock on before anything else happens. Deliberate self-control is a third source. Someone determined to show nothing often clamps down on all movement at once, and the result is a person who is suddenly and conspicuously calm. Research on deception has repeatedly found that, contrary to the stereotype of the fidgeting liar, people trying to control themselves tend to move their hands and fingers less, not more. Like every such cue the effect is small, and plenty of honest people do the same simply because they feel watched.

To notice stillness you need a baseline that includes movement. You cannot see a man stop gesturing if you never saw him gesture. This is one reason the first chapter of this book insists on watching people at ease before you watch them under any kind of question.

When you do notice it, slow down rather than speed up. A person who has gone still is often managing a great deal. The decent responses are the ones that lower the load: a pause, an easier question, a change of subject, a little more physical distance. If it was effort, you have given them room to think. If it was alarm, you have given them room to recover.
teach.disconfirm: If the person is still across easy and hard topics alike, stillness is their range, not a reaction. If the stillness comes while they are listening rather than speaking, it may simply be how they pay attention.

teach.h: What you see is theirs to explain and yours to protect.
teach.p:
Everything in this chapter can be misused, and the misuse is tempting because it feels clever. A negotiator who sees the other side's hand go to the neck when price is mentioned thinks he has found a weak point. A boss who notices an employee's foot freeze at a question about a project thinks he has found a lie. A partner who catalogues the other's self-touch during an argument thinks he has found proof. Each has found nothing but a person under strain, and each is about to make the strain worse.

The position of this book is simple. A pacifier is a person regulating themselves, and seeing it puts you under an obligation, not in a position of advantage. Lower the pressure. Slow down, sit back, offer an easier question or a way out. If you need to know more, ask openly and accept the answer you get. Never use what you noticed to press, corner or test someone. In a negotiation, treat the observation as information about the other side's constraints, something that might help you find an agreement both of you can live with, never as a lever.

There is one person whose pacifiers you are free to study as closely as you like: yourself. Your own hand at your neck in a meeting is twenty seconds of warning that most people never get. Learning your own repertoire, the jaw you rub, the thigh you smooth, the breath you hold, is the bridge between this chapter and the part of the book on the inner world. Men are often taught to ignore exactly these signals in themselves. Reading them is not weakness. It is the earliest information you will ever have about your own state.

See, then ease. That order never reverses.
teach.disconfirm: If, after you lower the pressure, the person's self-touch and stillness settle back toward their baseline, your attention was part of the strain. If they persist, the strain lies elsewhere; let them tell you about it, or not, in their own time.
teach.pullQuote: See, then ease. That order never reverses.

caseStudy:
Tom has led the mobile team at a mid-sized software company for two years. In meetings he talks with his hands: he draws architecture in the air, counts off risks on his fingers, leans back when he is confident. At the March planning review the director, Alan, asks whether the app will still ship on the fourteenth. Tom says yes. His hands, which have been moving all meeting, come down to his lap and stay there. His right thumb works across the knuckles of his left hand. His answers to the next three questions are a sentence each.

Alan has read a book on body language. He notes the stillness and the rubbing and concludes that Tom is hiding a slip. For the next twenty minutes he presses: *are you sure, what aren't you telling me, who else should I ask.* Tom grows quieter and more careful with each question, which Alan reads as confirmation. He leaves telling a colleague that Tom has lost control of the project.

Marcus, Tom's manager, was in the same room and saw the same things. He noted the change, the moment it began, and that it had not ended by the close of the meeting. He did not form a theory. Afterwards he walked Tom to the kitchen and said: *the fourteenth seemed to weigh on you. What would make it realistic?*

Tom exhaled. The app depended on a payments service owned by another team, whose lead had been on parental leave, and nothing had moved in three weeks. Tom had not wanted to name a colleague in front of the director. Marcus took it to the other team's manager that afternoon. The date moved by a week, with no blame and no surprise.

Both men saw the same leakage. One treated it as evidence and generated more of it. The other treated it as a pointer and asked where it pointed.
observe: Watch a televised press conference or a hard interview for ten minutes with the sound off, marking every self-touch with a rough timestamp. Then play it with sound and write down what had just been asked before each cluster, and before each quiet stretch.

In a meeting where you are not presenting, notice one colleague's ordinary gesturing in the first ten minutes. Afterwards, write down any moment their hands went still for more than a few seconds, what had just been said, and whether hard thinking was a plausible cause.

For one full day, catch your own pacifiers: each time you notice your hand at your face, neck, hair or thigh, write one word for what was happening just before. At the end of the day, look for the pattern.

In a queue, a waiting room or an airport gate, without staring at or recording anyone, notice which self-touches are most common among people who are simply waiting. That is the base rate you will compare everything else against.

drills.name: The Gradient
steps: Choose a five-minute clip of a seated interview in which the guest's whole body is visible.
Watch it once with a card covering everything below the guest's chin, and write three sentences about how they seem.
Watch it again with the face covered and only the body visible, and write three more sentences.
Compare the two descriptions and mark where they agree and where they differ.
For each difference, write one ordinary explanation that has nothing to do with concealment.
variations: Use a clip of someone you know personally, from a family video, and see whether their face and body tell the same story.
Try it with a clip of a sports post-match interview, where emotion is high and the face is heavily managed.
Do the face-only viewing with the sound on, then the body-only viewing with it off, and compare the effect of the voice.

drills.name: Rate, Not Instance
steps: Pick a long interview or panel in which one person is on camera for at least twenty minutes.
For the first ten minutes, tally the person's self-touches in one-minute blocks to find their resting rate.
For the next ten minutes keep tallying, and mark any minute at least double the resting rate.
For each spike, note what had been said in the preceding fifteen seconds.
Write one sentence per spike stating the pointer, not a meaning: something about this topic cost effort.
variations: Repeat with a second person in the same panel and compare their baselines and spikes.
Try tallying a different behaviour, such as posture shifts, and see whether its spikes line up with the self-touch spikes.

drills.name: Effort or Strain
steps: Write six questions on cards: three easy, such as what you ate yesterday, and three demanding, such as the months in reverse order or the plot of the last book you read.
Set your phone to record yourself from the waist up, shuffle the cards, and answer each one aloud.
Watch the recording with the sound off and mark every change in your hands, gaze and posture.
Match each change to its question and count how many came during the demanding ones.
Write down which of these changes an observer might have mistaken for discomfort or evasion.
variations: Ask a friend to choose the questions without telling you which are which, and see whether you can tell from the recording.
Add a seventh card with a mildly embarrassing question, and compare your body's response with the difficult ones.

drills.name: Your Pacifier Map
steps: Sit somewhere quiet and recall, in detail, a recent moment that embarrassed you or a conversation you are dreading.
Stay with it for two minutes without trying to control your body.
Notice where your hands went, what your breath did and where your shoulders sat, and write each down.
Repeat with a pleasant memory and note the differences.
Write your three likeliest pacifiers on a card and keep it in your wallet for a week.
variations: Repeat after a stressful day at work, and compare which pacifiers appear first when you are already tired.
Ask someone close to you which of your pacifiers they have noticed, and compare their list with yours.

drills.name: Ease, Not Press
steps: Recall a recent conversation in which someone seemed uncomfortable at a particular moment.
Write down exactly what you said and did in the minute after you noticed.
Mark each of your moves as easing the pressure or adding to it.
Rewrite that minute using only easing moves: a pause, a simpler question, an offered exit, a little more distance.
Say the rewritten version aloud once, so that it is available to you next time.
variations: Rewrite a second conversation, this time one in which you were the one under strain, and note what would have helped you.
Practise one easing move this week in a real conversation, and note how the other person responded.

quiz.q: A man touches the front of his neck while answering whether he finished a report. What does the research support concluding?
options: He is probably lying about the report, since neck touching is a classic sign of deceit
He is probably anxious about the report and worried about what you will say next
Something may have registered or cost effort, if it departs from his baseline and follows the question
Nothing at all, since self-touch is a meaningless habit that everyone has all day
quiz.explain: No single self-touch is a sign of lying, and anxiety is only one of several possible causes. The last option overcorrects: a well-timed departure from someone's baseline is information, just not an answer. The defensible claim is the narrow one.

quiz.q: In Ekman and Friesen's account of leakage, why is the face the channel least likely to let unmanaged feeling escape?
options: The face can show fewer distinct emotions than the body, so there is less to leak
People watch faces most and get the most feedback about them, so they manage them best
Facial muscles move more slowly than leg muscles, so leaks are too brief to notice
Faces only show emotion clearly in young children, before display rules have been learned
quiz.explain: The argument rests on sending capacity, attention and feedback. We are watched in the face and know it, so we control it most. The legs and feet are watched least, which makes them likelier to show what is not being managed, though not necessarily anything concealed.

quiz.q: During a salary negotiation, the other side's lead rubs the back of his neck twice as you name your figure, then goes still. What is the most defensible next move?
options: Hold silence and steady eye contact to see whether he breaks first
Note the change and ask an open question about their constraints
Raise your figure, since the rubbing shows he is clearly rattled
Point out to him that he seems uncomfortable with your number
quiz.explain: The touch and the stillness point to effort or pressure near that moment, not to a weakness you can exploit. An open question about constraints lets you learn what the pressure is about and keeps the negotiation honest. Silence and staring are pressure, and pressure produces more of the signals you think you are reading.

quiz.q: Bond and DePaulo's meta-analysis of deception judgments found that people's average accuracy was about:
options: 54 percent
75 percent
90 percent for trained observers
33 percent
quiz.explain: Across more than two hundred studies, people told lies from truths only slightly better than chance. Trained professionals did not reliably do better. Leakage is real, but it is not a lie detector.

quiz.q: Which statement about stillness is best supported?
options: Liars fidget more than truth-tellers, so stillness is a fairly good sign of honesty
Stillness is never informative, because it is an absence of behaviour, not a signal
A sudden drop in someone's usual movement can be informative, with several possible causes
Stillness nearly always indicates fear, since freezing is the oldest threat response
quiz.explain: The fidgeting liar is a stereotype; research tends to find that people controlling themselves move their hands less, not more. But stillness has many causes, so it is a pointer, never a verdict. You can only see it at all if you know how much the person usually moves.

quiz.q: Your own hand keeps going to your jaw during a tense conversation with your father about his finances. What is the most useful response?
options: Suppress it, so that he does not read it as a sign that you are losing the argument
Treat it as early information about your own state: breathe out and slow the conversation down
Point out that he seems tense too, so that the two of you are on an equal footing
Ignore it, since self-touch is a meaningless habit and says nothing about your state
quiz.explain: Your own pacifiers are the earliest signal you will ever have about your state. Suppressing them removes the information without removing the strain. Using them to regulate yourself, and the pace of the conversation, is the skill this chapter is built toward.

quiz.q: A colleague says that touching your nose while talking is a reliable sign of lying. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since a nose touch is one of the best-established signs of deception there is
A nose touch has many causes, and at most shows strain at a moment, not that anything is false
He is right only when the nose touch comes with a glance away, which completes the cluster
Nose touches mean nothing at all, since they are always caused by colds or by allergies
quiz.explain: Self-touch, including touching the nose, is common and has many causes. At best, a change from baseline at a marked moment tells you that something cost effort, and even trained observers detect lies only a little better than chance.

quiz.q: What did Mohiyeddini and Semple's study of displacement behaviour in men suggest?
options: That self-touching under stress made the men feel more stressed, by drawing their attention to it
That self-touching had no relationship at all with how stressed the men said they felt afterwards
That self-touching under stress may help regulate it, with more of it linked to less felt stress
That only men who were lying showed any increase in self-touching while they were under stress
quiz.explain: Men who showed more displacement behaviour, such as self-touching, under stress reported less stress, which suggests the behaviour does real work. That is one reason why suppressing your own pacifiers tends to backfire.

quiz.q: Each time you call on a quiet pupil without warning, she pulls her sleeves over her hands and her jiggling foot goes still. What fits this chapter best?
options: Call on her more often, so that she gets used to answering in front of the whole class
Tell her to take her hands out of her sleeves, so that she learns better classroom habits
Mention to her parents that she seems sullen and may not be trying hard enough in class
Give her warning before you ask her, and reduce the pressure rather than add to it
quiz.explain: The pacifiers and the stillness point to a moment of strain, being called on without warning. Using the reading to make things easier, with a warning and time, is what this chapter recommends.

quiz.q: You notice your own jaw working and your pen tapping during a tense conversation with your father. What does this chapter suggest?
options: Notice them early, and deal with the strain itself through breath and a pause, without fighting them
Clamp your jaw and hands still, so that your father cannot see that you are under any strain
Ignore them, since your own pacifiers are private and cannot affect how the other person feels
Point them out to your father, so that he understands how difficult you find the conversation
quiz.explain: Your own pacifiers leak into the room and change how others respond. Suppressing them tends to produce other signs of strain, so the better course is to notice them and ease the strain underneath.

reflection.prompt: Describe one specific moment in the last month when you noticed your own body soothing itself: a hand at your neck, a rubbed jaw, a held breath, palms slid down your thighs. Where were you, who was there, and what had just happened? Then describe what you did next, and whether noticing the touch changed anything. If you did not notice it at the time, write about how you realised it afterwards.
reflection.guidance: Be as physical as you can: which hand, which part of you, for how long. Resist explaining the moment away, and resist dramatising it. The aim is to begin a map of your own pacifiers, because you will use it in the chapters on stress, anger and anxiety, and because it is the one map of leakage you are entitled to draw in full. If this feels hard, remember that noticing a pacifier is not admitting a weakness. It is catching yourself in the act of looking after yourself.

failureMode: The commonest failure with this chapter is the pacifier hunt. A reader who has learned the taxonomy starts scanning for neck touches and jaw rubs and, finding them everywhere, because they are everywhere, decides that everyone is anxious about something and that he can see it. He has confused frequency with significance. Worse, he usually begins to act on what he finds, pressing where he sees strain, which produces more strain and more pacifiers, which feel like confirmation. The second failure is reading pacifiers as deception. Nothing in the research supports a neck touch as a sign of lying in particular; it is a sign of effort, discomfort or habit in roughly everyone. If you catch yourself thinking *there's the tell*, stop, and ask instead what would make this moment easier for the person in front of you.

moreCases.title: Palms on the thighs
moreCases.scene:
In a job interview for an operations role, Daniel answers the first questions easily. When the interviewer, Fiona, asks about a nine-month
  gap on his CV, his hands, which have been resting on the table, slide down under it, and she sees his forearms move as he rubs his palms along
  his thighs, twice, slowly. He answers that he took time out for family reasons, then adds that he spent some of it doing a course. His voice is
  steady, but the answer is shorter than his others.

  Fiona has been on a course about body language in interviews. She knows the leg rub as a pacifying behaviour and has heard it described as a
  sign that someone is uncomfortable with what they are saying. She writes in the margin: gap, evasive, check references carefully. For the rest of
  the interview she is cooler and asks two further questions about the gap, each a little more pointed. Daniel's answers get shorter.

After the interview, Fiona's colleague, who sat in, says that she thought Daniel seemed strong. Fiona says that the gap bothered her, and that his body language did not help. When her colleague asks what exactly he did, Fiona says he went quiet and rubbed his legs, and realises as she says it how little that is.
moreCases.misread:
Fiona read a pacifier as a sign of concealment and then pressed on the point where she saw strain, which is the misuse this chapter most warns against. The pressing produced more strain and shorter answers, which she then took as confirmation.

She also treated a question about personal circumstances as a test of honesty, which it was never fit to be.
moreCases.betterRead:
The leg rub was a real pointer, arriving within a second or two of a specific question, and it did tell Fiona something: the gap cost Daniel some effort to talk about. It did not tell her why. There are many reasons a person might find a gap hard to discuss: illness, a breakdown, caring for a dying parent, a redundancy they are ashamed of, a prison sentence, a pregnancy that ended badly. Most of them are none of an interviewer's business beyond what the job requires. The careful response was to note the pointer, accept the answer, and move on, or, if the gap mattered for the role, to ask one neutral question about what he had been doing to keep his skills current. Daniel had, it later emerged, been caring for his mother through cancer. He did not get the job, and Fiona's notes were part of the reason.

A pointer is a reason for care, not suspicion. In an interview, care means accepting a brief answer about a personal matter, and judging the candidate on what the job requires.

moreCases.title: Sleeves over the hands
moreCases.scene:
Mr Adeyemi teaches maths to a Year 9 class. He notices that one pupil, Megan, pulls her jumper sleeves down over her hands whenever he
  asks the class a question, and grips the cuffs from inside. When he calls on her by name, her foot, which has been jiggling under the desk,
  stops dead, and she stares at her book. She usually answers that she does not know. Her written work is good.

  Some teachers would read Megan's behaviour as sullenness or a lack of effort, and some of her previous teachers have. Mr Adeyemi tries
  something different. For two weeks he stops calling on Megan without warning. Instead, before asking the class a question, he tells her quietly,
  as he passes her desk, that he will ask her about the next one. When the question comes, her sleeves stay where they are and she answers,
  correctly, in a quiet voice. By the end of the term she occasionally puts her hand up.

Mr Adeyemi also notices that on days when Megan has had a warning, her sleeves stay down for the whole lesson, not just the moment of the question. The fear of being called on had been colouring the entire hour.
moreCases.misread:
The common misreading of a child like Megan is to take the pacifiers, the sleeves and the frozen foot, as a sign that she is withdrawn by temperament or simply not trying, and to respond by pressing harder: calling on her more, insisting she speak up, telling her to take her hands out of her sleeves.

Each of those responses would have increased the very strain the pacifiers were managing, and taught Megan that being noticed meant being pressed.
moreCases.betterRead:
Her pacifiers were pointers to a specific moment, being called on without warning in front of the class, and the stillness of her foot pointed to the same moment. Read that way, they suggested strain at the prospect of public performance, not a lack of knowledge or effort, and the written work supported that. Mr Adeyemi used the reading the way this chapter recommends: to reduce the pressure rather than to apply more. A warning, a little time, a quieter way to answer. He never mentioned the sleeves, never asked her to stop, and never told her what he had seen. The point of noticing was to change what he did.

A year later, Megan's form tutor mentions that she has started speaking in assemblies. Nobody connects it to the maths lessons, and nobody needs to.

moreCases.title: The hand at the back of his neck
moreCases.scene:
Over a few months, Sarah notices that her husband, Liam, rubs the back of his neck whenever his mother is mentioned. He does it when his
  sister rings, when Sarah suggests visiting, and once when a television advert shows an elderly woman in a care home. He does not do it at other
  times. When she asks how his mother is, he says she is fine, getting older, nothing to worry about.

  Sarah does not tell Liam what she has noticed. She does not say that his body is telling her something different from his words. Instead, one
  Sunday when they are walking the dog, she says that she has been wondering how his mum is really getting on, and that she would like to go with
  him next time he visits. Liam is quiet for a while. Then he says that his mother has been forgetting things, leaving the gas on, getting lost
  on the way to the shops she has used for forty years, and that he has been too frightened to say it out loud.

Afterwards, Sarah wonders how long Liam would have carried it alone if she had not asked. She also wonders how close she came to asking the wrong way, at the dinner table, in front of the children, with the words "you always do that when I mention your mum".
moreCases.misread:
A less careful partner might have read the neck rub as irritation with his mother, or as something Liam was hiding, and confronted him with it: every time I mention your mum you do that, what aren't you telling me? Or she might have dismissed it as a habit and taken his words at face value.

Either response would have been a mistake: the first would have made Liam defend himself, and the second would have left him alone with it.
moreCases.betterRead:
The neck rub was a pacifier with a consistent pointer: the same topic, many times, and not otherwise. That made it worth acting on, but only in the way this chapter allows. A pacifier tells you where the pressure is, never what it is. Sarah used it to choose a topic and a moment, and then asked an open question, side by side, with an offer attached. She left the explaining to Liam, which is where it belonged, and gave him a setting in which explaining was easier. Months later, Liam told her that he had been waiting for someone to ask, and that he could not have started the conversation himself.

The same approach works with friends, colleagues and children: a repeated pacifier at a repeated topic tells you where to look, and the most respectful way to look is to offer an open door, not to point at what you saw.

moreCases.title: Your own jaw
moreCases.scene:
Craig, forty-five, sits with his father at the kitchen table to talk about his father's finances, which have become muddled since his mother
  died. His father is proud and defensive. Halfway through, Craig's sister, who is listening on speakerphone, says afterwards that she could hear
  in Craig's voice how angry he was. Craig is surprised; he thought he was being patient.

  That evening, he watches a recording he had made of the conversation, with his father's permission, to keep track of the figures. He sees
  himself working his jaw from side to side, rubbing his chin with the knuckles of one hand, sighing through his nose before answering, and gripping
  his pen so that it taps the table. His father, across the table, looks at Craig's hands each time they move and becomes more defensive each
  time.

Craig also notices, watching the recording, that his father's own hands are still for most of the conversation, except when Craig's move. His father had been watching him far more closely than Craig had been watching his father.

Watching it back, Craig counts eleven sighs in forty minutes. He has no memory of any of them. He does remember feeling, throughout, that he was being the patient one, and that his father was making things difficult for no reason.
moreCases.misread:
Craig had been watching his father's body for signs of confusion or distress, and had not noticed his own at all. He thought his pacifiers were private, a way of managing his own frustration. His father read them as impatience and disapproval, and responded to them.

He had also assumed that his impatience was invisible because he had kept it out of his words, which is the same mistake he would have made if he had read his father's words and ignored his hands.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter's final teaching point says that what you see in others is theirs to explain and yours to protect, and the same holds for what others see in you. Your own pacifiers leak into the room and change the conversation. The defence is not to suppress them, which tends to produce stiffness and other leakage, but to notice them early and deal with the strain underneath: a slow breath out, shoulders down, hands resting open on the table, a pause before answering. Craig tried it the following week, with a card in his pocket listing his three pacifiers. When he felt his jaw start to work, he breathed out and put his pen down. His father noticed nothing, but the conversation went better.

He also found, a little to his surprise, that the slow breath helped him as much as it helped the conversation. His frustration with his father was real, but it had been amplified by the strain of holding it in.

workedReading.title: The foot that stopped
workedReading.scene:
You are in the pub with your friend Alex. As usual, his right foot is bouncing under the table, a steady jiggle that you have seen at every pint for ten years. He is telling a funny story about work, hands moving. You mention, in passing, that you saw his ex, Hannah, at a friend's party last weekend with her new partner. The foot stops dead. His hands come down to the table and wrap around his glass. He says, "Oh, right. Good for her," and takes a long drink. A few seconds later the foot starts again, faster than before.

Alex and Hannah split up six months ago, and Alex has said almost nothing about it since, except that it was for the best.

steps.label: Know the baseline
steps.text:
The bouncing foot is Alex's baseline, as reliable as his laugh. Its stopping is therefore the change, not its presence. If you did not know him, you might have read the bouncing as nerves all evening and missed the moment that mattered. This is why stillness, as the chapter says, can leak more than movement.

Knowing the baseline also saves you from the opposite error. All evening the bouncing foot has meant nothing, and you have not read anything into it.

steps.label: Mark the timing
steps.text:
The foot stopped within a second of a specific phrase: Hannah, with her new partner. The hands came to the glass at the same moment, and the drink followed. When the foot restarted, it was faster. Changes in three channels, at a named moment, make this a pointer rather than noise.

The restarting, faster, is part of the pointer too. Something that was held for a moment has been released, and with more energy than before.

steps.label: Read the pointer, not a meaning
steps.text:
Something about the mention of Hannah, or her new partner, or the party, or your having seen her, cost Alex effort. That is all the pointer says. It does not tell you whether he is hurt, jealous, relieved, embarrassed or simply caught off guard. The pacifier, gripping the glass and drinking, is the body managing whatever it was.

It is tempting to fill in the meaning from what you know, that they split up recently. Resist it. Your knowledge narrows the possibilities without choosing among them.

steps.label: Consider effort
steps.text:
Could it be mental effort rather than feeling? Possibly: he may be trying to remember who the new partner is, or working out how to respond politely. But effort usually comes with looking away and slowing speech, and Alex answered quickly and shortly, which fits managing a feeling better than searching for a thought.

Considering effort at all is a useful habit, because it reminds you that not every change is a feeling.

steps.label: Decide whether to ease or press
steps.text:
You could press: ask how he feels about it, say that he seemed bothered. That would put him on the spot in a pub, with the pacifier still working. Or you could ease: let the moment pass, change the subject back to his story, and leave the door open for later. The chapter is clear that a pointer is a reason to make things easier, not harder.

It is worth noticing how strong the urge to press can be when you care about someone. You want to help, and helping feels like getting him to talk. Often it is the opposite.

steps.label: Ease, and leave a door
steps.text:
You say that you only saw her briefly, and ask what happened next with his boss. Alex picks up the story, and his hands start moving again. Later, walking to the bus, you say that it must still be strange hearing about Hannah, and that you are around if he ever wants to talk about it. You say it once and do not repeat it.

The single, light offer, made side by side on the walk, gives him something he can come back to without making him respond now.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Alex says nothing that night. A month later, after a five-a-side game, he tells you that the break-up had been his idea and that he had regretted it almost immediately, and that hearing about the new partner had been the first time he had admitted to himself that it was over. The foot had pointed you to the topic. Easing, and the door you left, let him choose when to walk through it.

It is also worth noticing what you never did: you never told Alex that his foot had stopped. He never needed to know that you had noticed.

moreFailures.title: Suppressing your own pacifiers
moreFailures.body:
Readers who learn that their self-touch is visible often try to stop it: sitting on their hands in interviews, clamping their legs still, forcing their hands away from their faces. This tends to backfire. Pacifiers do real work in regulating strain, and the evidence this chapter describes suggests that self-touch under stress may help. Suppressing them leaves the strain without its outlet, and it often shows up somewhere else instead: a rigid posture, a held breath, a tight voice, a foot that taps harder because the hands are pinned. A better approach is to work on the strain itself: breathe out slowly, drop the shoulders, rest the hands loosely and openly where they can move if they need to. A pacifier you allow is far less noticeable than one you are fighting.

If you find yourself in a situation where a pacifier would be genuinely distracting, such as giving a speech, choose a quiet one in advance, such as resting one hand lightly on the lectern, rather than trying to have none at all.

moreFailures.title: Treating pacifiers as a lie detector
moreFailures.body:
Many popular books and courses present the neck touch, the nose rub and the leg rub as signs of deception. They are signs of strain, and strain has many sources, including being suspected of something you did not do. Bond and DePaulo's analysis of deception research, described in this chapter's quiz, found people detecting lies at little better than chance, and nothing in the research on self-touch suggests a way around that. A man who touches his neck while denying something may be lying, or frightened of not being believed, or embarrassed by the question, or simply someone who touches his neck a great deal. The deception chapter later in this part explains why trying to catch lies from the body does more harm than good.

There is a further cost. People who have been taught that self-touch reveals lies sometimes start to watch their own hands anxiously in honest conversations, which makes them look exactly as uncomfortable as they fear.

moreFailures.title: Mistaking a body's needs for a mind's strain
moreFailures.body:
Not every touch is a pacifier. People scratch because they itch, from eczema, allergies, insect bites or dry skin. They rub their eyes because they are tired or wear contact lenses. They touch their noses because they have a cold. They fidget because they have ADHD, or because they need to move to concentrate, or because they stopped smoking last week. Some people have tics. Many autistic people stim, repeating movements that help them regulate, and Part V's chapter on neurodivergence explains why stopping those movements can cost them a great deal. Before reading self-touch as strain, ask whether the body has a simpler reason, and whether the movement is part of this person's normal range.

When in doubt, look at the rate over time. A body's needs tend to produce steady patterns, such as scratching throughout a meeting, while strain tends to produce spikes at particular moments.

A colleague who scratches her arm through every meeting has told you something about her skin, not her conscience. The pointer only becomes interesting when the pattern changes.

moreFailures.title: Pressing on the pressure point
moreFailures.body:
The most damaging misuse of this chapter is the one it was written to prevent: seeing a pacifier at a particular topic and using it as a weak spot. A negotiator who sees the other side's hand go to their neck when a deadline is mentioned, and then keeps returning to the deadline. A manager who sees an employee freeze at a question and keeps asking it. A partner who notices the other's discomfort about a subject and brings it up in every argument. Each is using what they read to increase someone's distress for advantage. It may work in the short term. It is also exactly what the ethics statement at the front of this book refuses, and it corrodes every relationship it touches.

If you notice that you have done this, the repair is the same as any other wrong: stop, acknowledge it if you can, and change how you use what you see.

It is worth remembering that the person under strain often knows exactly what you are doing, even if they cannot name it, and remembers it long after the negotiation or the argument is over.

questions.q: Is touching your nose a sign that you are lying?
questions.a:
No. The idea comes partly from the story of Pinocchio and partly from popular writing that presented nose touching as a classic sign of deception, sometimes with a story about the nose becoming engorged when people lie. The evidence does not support it as a reliable sign. People touch their noses when they itch, when they have colds, when they are thinking, when they are uncomfortable, and when they are lying, and the last is no more common than the others. Like every pacifier, a nose touch is worth noting only as a change from baseline at a marked moment, and even then it tells you that something cost effort, not that something was false.

If you want a useful rule, it is this: the more famous a body-language sign is for lying, the less you should trust it.

questions.q: Should I try to hide my own pacifiers in an interview?
questions.a:
No; try to reduce the strain instead. Interviewers who know anything about this will expect candidates to touch their faces, shift and rub their hands; it is normal in a stressful setting, and good interviewers discount it. What helps is preparation that reduces strain at the source: practising your answers to the questions you dread most, especially about gaps or failures, until you can say them calmly. On the day, breathe out slowly before you answer, rest your hands loosely on your lap or the table, and give yourself permission to pause. If your hands still go to your neck now and then, let them.

If an interviewer ever comments on your hands or face, you are entitled to steer back to the substance: you were thinking, and here is your answer.

It can help to remember that the interviewer is also under some strain, and probably touching their own face too.

questions.q: How can I tell effort from distress?
questions.a:
Often you cannot, from the body alone, but there are clues. Effort tends to come with looking away, slower speech, pauses and a return to baseline once the thinking is done. Distress tends to come with changes in voice, breathing and facial tension, and may linger after the topic has moved on. Timing helps: changes that come with a hard question, such as a calculation or a memory test, lean towards effort, while changes that come with an emotionally loaded topic lean towards strain. The honest answer, as so often in this book, is to allow for both and to ask in a way that leaves room for either.

With people you know well, you will gradually learn their particular patterns. Some people go quiet when they think and loud when they are upset; others the reverse.

questions.q: What should I do when I notice someone is under strain?
questions.a:
Make things easier, in small ways, without announcing it. Slow your own pace. Leave a pause. Ask a simpler or more open question, or move to a different topic for a while and come back later. Offer a break, a glass of water, or a way to finish the conversation another time. If you are in a position of power over the person, as an interviewer, manager, teacher or officer, be especially careful, because they cannot easily ask for these things themselves. What you should not do is tell them what you have seen, ask why they touched their neck, or press harder on the topic. The point of noticing strain is to reduce it.

It is worth practising these moves in ordinary conversations, so that they are available to you when a conversation becomes difficult. Under pressure, people do what they have practised.

Children pacify constantly, and many of their pacifiers are the adult ones in plainer form: thumb sucking, hair twirling, chewing sleeves, pulling jumpers over hands, rocking, holding a favourite object. They are normal, and most fade or change form with age. Shaming a child for them, or forcing them to stop, removes a way of coping without addressing whatever made coping necessary. If a child's pacifiers increase sharply, or appear in new settings, treat it as you would a change in an adult's baseline: notice when it happens, think about what has changed in their life, and ask gently, perhaps side by side, perhaps through play.

Teenagers often move their pacifiers to their phones: scrolling, turning the phone over, checking it without reading. The same rule applies. Notice the timing, and ask rather than confiscate.

questions.q: Do pacifiers differ from person to person?
questions.a:
Very much. Most people have a small repertoire of favourites, often two or three, which they use far more than others: one person rubs the back of the neck, another touches the lips, another smooths their trousers or turns a ring. These habits are surprisingly stable over years, which is why the drill in this chapter asks you to map your own. It also means that learning the pacifiers of the people you see most often is far more useful than learning a general list. A neck touch from someone who never touches their neck means more than a neck touch from someone who does it twenty times an hour.

It also means that two people can use the same movement for very different reasons. Your colleague's chin rub may be her thinking face; your brother's may be his tell for irritation.

watch.title: Behaviors That Tell You Something Is Wrong
watch.notice: Joe Navarro, who popularised the term pacifiers, describes behaviours that suggest discomfort. Watch for the neck touches, lip compressions and self-soothing he names, and remember that they show discomfort, not its cause.

reviewPrompt: Watch two minutes of a public figure answering hard questions with the sound off and list every self-touch with a timestamp. Then turn the sound on and write what each cluster followed, with one ordinary explanation for each.
